title: These Planets Are Lighter Than Cotton Candy!
summary: Have you ever held cotton candy and felt how light it is? Now imagine a whole planet that's even lighter! Astronomers just found two planets that are fluffier than cotton candy. They're called TOI-791 b and TOI-791 c, and they're about 1,110 light-years away from Earth. That's really far — a light-year is the distance light travels in one year, which is almost 6 trillion miles! These planets are huge, each about the size of Jupiter, the biggest planet in our solar system. But they're super lightweight. Jupiter is like a heavy bowling ball compared to them. In fact, Jupiter is about 30 times denser. Density is how much stuff is packed into a certain space. Cotton candy has a density of about 0.05 grams per cubic centimeter. TOI-791 b is even less dense, at just 0.038! That means if you could put it in a giant swimming pool, it would float. The two planets are like siblings, born from the same cloud of gas and dust. They dance around their star in a special pattern: for every five laps the inner planet makes, the outer one does three. Their gravity tugs on each other, which helped scientists figure out their masses. Volunteers, regular people like you, first spotted these planets in data from a NASA telescope. Then astronomers used telescopes all over the world, even one in Antarctica, to learn more. The long, dark Antarctic winter let them watch the planets pass in front of their star for over 11 hours without stopping. Scientists think these puffy planets have huge, lightweight atmospheres made of hydrogen and helium. They might have formed far from their star, where it was cold enough to gather all that gas. Now, researchers want to study them more to understand how such strange worlds come to be.
why_it_matters: Finding planets so different from anything in our solar system shows we still have so much to learn about how worlds are born, and it might inspire you to one day explore the stars yourself.

keywords.explanation: A light-year is how far light travels in one year — almost 6 trillion miles, used to measure huge distances in space.
Density tells you how tightly packed the stuff inside something is; cotton candy has low density, rocks have high density.
An atmosphere is the layer of gas surrounding a planet, like the air around Earth.
Hydrogen is the lightest and simplest gas in the universe, and it makes up most of the Sun.
Helium is a very light gas that makes balloons float; it's also found in stars and giant planets.
Gravity is the invisible force that pulls things toward each other — it keeps planets in orbit and holds us on the ground.

background_read: Planets outside our solar system are called exoplanets, and astronomers have already found thousands of them — some hot, some icy, but very few as light as cotton candy.
Jupiter (the biggest planet in our solar system) is a gas giant, but it is still much denser than these newly discovered worlds.

Special telescopes like the one in Antarctica can stare at the same patch of sky for months during the dark winter, helping scientists spot tiny dips in starlight when a planet passes in front of its star.
Article_Structure: WHO: Astronomers around the world, NASA citizen volunteers, and scientists using telescopes including one in Antarctica
WHAT: Discovery of two huge but extremely lightweight exoplanets (TOI-791 b and TOI-791 c), fluffier than cotton candy, with low density
WHERE: Orbiting a star about 1,110 light-years from Earth, in a special orbital dance
WHY: To understand how such strange, puffy planets form and how their lightweight atmospheres of hydrogen and helium came to be

perspectives.description: This is an amazing chance to study how planets can be so light — it challenges our ideas and opens new questions about planet formation.
Ordinary people like me helped make a real discovery, and that feels incredible — science isn't only for professionals.
We still need to learn much more; these planets are so far away that we can't see them directly, so our ideas about their atmospheres might change with more data.
